abstract: This study introduces the concept of 'Deceptive Information Operations' (DIOs) as an analytical framework that moves beyond traditional false-news taxonomies to capture a broader spectrum of manipulative communicative activities on social media. Using an automated detection workflow that monitors coordinated sharing behaviour on Facebook, the authors analyse three cases: a state-aligned pro-Putin propaganda network, a coordinated online gambling promotion campaign, and a network of poorly moderated public groups distributing adult content and fraudulent links. Each case is examined across three dimensions—deceptive content, exploitation of platform affordances, and participatory behaviours—revealing shared structural mechanisms that echo the notion of a 'Zombie Internet.' The paper argues that current platform governance frameworks fail because they focus narrowly on content inauthenticity rather than the structural conditions enabling manipulation at scale.
key_claims: Traditional taxonomies of false news and existing frameworks (deception theory, strategic information operations, coordinated inauthentic behaviour) each capture only one dimension of contemporary manipulation and are individually insufficient.

Deceptive Information Operations (DIOs) are defined by the convergence of three dimensions—deceptive intent in content and identity, strategic exploitation of platform affordances, and multi-account coordination—rather than by the presence of false content, which is neither necessary nor sufficient.

Structurally distinct operations pursuing different harms (epistemic, economic, social-normative) share a common underlying operational logic, making motivational distinctions analytically secondary to structural logic.

Facebook's engagement-driven design and inconsistent moderation create the conditions of a 'Zombie Internet' where the boundary between human and automated, authentic and manipulated activity becomes difficult to sustain.
Meta's enforcement categories (CIB and CSH) are drawn too narrowly and cannot recognise harmful operations whose effectiveness is not reducible to coordination-plus-inauthenticity.
methods: Purposive case selection (Palys, 2008) of three cases from 17 networks detected by the vera.ai monitoring workflow, chosen for typological, actor, and coordination-mechanism diversity representing epistemic, economic, and social-normative harm.

An automated, adaptive detection workflow (VeraAI Alert System) using CooRTweet to detect synchronous sharing, seeded from 1,225 fact-checker-flagged Facebook accounts and a corpus of 36,091 pages flagged false by Meta's fact-checking partners (2017-2022).

Data collection via the Meta Content Library (one of the first studies to use it at scale), analysing account-level metadata plus the 500 most-viewed posts per network within October 2023-August 2024.

Inductive category development informed by constructivist grounded theory (Charmaz, 2014; Starbird et al., 2023), with three theoretically motivated dimensions (identity management, behavioural coordination, content manipulation) and inductively emergent categories.

Coding reliability procedures: each case assigned a primary coder, the lead author cross-coded 30% of the dataset, and coding decisions were reviewed collaboratively; a codebook (Table A1) documents operational definitions.
findings: Pro-Putin network: 27 public groups showing replicated naming conventions, synchronised name changes preceding geopolitical events, and coordinated posting (e.g., an anti-Zelenskyy meme shared across six groups within a six-minute window, accumulating over 1.1 million views); blends AI-generated heroic imagery of Putin with benign urban-development content to obscure intent.

Gambling network: 260 groups (30,000 to ~600,000 members) using automation and generative AI, with some groups producing up to 10,000 posts per month; posts show anomalous metrics (e.g., 169.1K views, 44.1K comments, 7 reactions, 0 shares) indicating artificial comment inflation and largely synthetic engagement, plus brandjacking of names like Orion Stars and Juwa; 368 of the 500 top posts were removed by analysis time.

Unmoderated groups: 222 groups forming two communities, exploiting weak moderation; accounts repeatedly renamed (one group changed names 13 times), and adult content disguised via 'listening to' activity-status links, empty Musician/Band pages, and unrelated BMW-history blurbs with tinyurl links to evade CIB detection; a Coca-Cola alcohol hoax reached 3.5 million views and 37,300 shares.

Cross-case synthesis: all three conceal intent behind benign content, rely on coordinated sharing and synthetic/AI-generated material, and exploit engagement-driven ranking, but differ in user engagement (genuine amplification, near-total synthetic activity, and inadvertent user amplification respectively).

Facebook's enforcement framework failed across all cases to reliably distinguish automated from genuine participation or deceptive from legitimate content; the authors' reports to Meta in October 2023 and November 2024 received acknowledgement but limited follow-up action.
contributions: Proposes the Deceptive Information Operations (DIOs) framework, synthesising deception theory, strategic information operations, and coordinated inauthentic behaviour into a single analytical lens.
Provides an empirically grounded conceptualisation demonstrating that operations differing in actor, content, and intent share a common structural logic.
Identifies critical gaps in platform governance frameworks that focus on content inauthenticity rather than structural enabling conditions, with direct evidence of enforcement failure.
Offers a codebook and an automated, cyclical detection workflow enabling researchers and civil society to monitor coordinated deceptive activity at scale using the Meta Content Library.
Empirically operationalises Koebler's (2024) 'Zombie Internet' concept as a systemic ecosystem condition emerging from engagement-oriented design.
framing: The paper positions itself within scholarship on online manipulation, information disorder, and platform governance, bridging three fragmented bodies of theory—Chadwick and Stanyer's (2022) deception theory, Starbird et al.'s (2019) strategic information operations, and Meta's Coordinated Inauthentic Behaviour framework (Gleicher, 2018). It frames deceptive operations as an emergent property of engagement-driven platform design ('Zombie Internet') that exceeds the boundaries of current disinformation taxonomies and regulatory categories.
